extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, undergraduate mathematics instructors, and curriculum designers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, implementing, and evaluating an inquiry-oriented undergraduate differential equations course (IO-DE) and comparing student beliefs, routine skills, and conceptual understanding to traditional instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry-oriented classroom (social norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a learning environment where students routinely offer explanations of and justifications for their reasoning; examples of social norms include routinely explaining to and listening to others, questioning others’ thinking, and responding to others’ questions and challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being intentional about fostering such norms is a pedagogical goal of IO-DE classrooms. These discursive regularities are constituted and reconstituted through ongoing interaction and should be cultivated through small-group work and whole-class discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociomathematical norms (criteria for mathematical explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociomathematical norms refer to criteria for what counts as an acceptable explanation, a different explanation, and as an elegant justification; they are not pre-set rules but emerge as joint accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should encourage emergence of these norms and use them to complement social norms as mechanisms by which teaching for understanding occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided reinvention (heuristic for task design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate instructional starting points that are experientially real to students and take into account students’ current mathematical ways of knowing; examine students’ informal solution strategies to suggest pathways to develop more formal practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include historical examinations of how concepts evolved and consider technology-enabled starting points that history would not reveal. Use guided reinvention to scaffold students toward formal constructs (e.g., students reinventing Euler’s method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergent models (heuristic for sequencing tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design connected, long-term series of problems in which students create and elaborate symbolic models (number tables, algorithms, graphs, analytic expressions) that evolve from informal activity to models for reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coherent sequence alone does not guarantee understanding; tasks must be theoretically informed and iteratively tested in classrooms to foster mathematization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dynamical systems perspective for content selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat differential equations as mechanisms describing how functions evolve and change over time; focus on long-term behavior of solutions, number and nature of equilibria, effect of varying parameters, and systems of differential equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize interpretation and characterization of solution behavior rather than exclusively finding closed-form symbolic solutions; include systems and higher-order concerns appropriate to real-world phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology as a tool, not an end
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical and numerical techniques (slope fields, vector fields, Euler’s method, numerical algorithms) should emerge as tools students use to solve challenging problems rather than being taught as ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technology (e.g., Java applets) to support reinvention and conceptual development (e.g., re-inventing bifurcation diagrams or eigenvector concepts) while ensuring tasks make the tool use meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional tasks constitute as important as content
rubrics_metrics.description: How instructional tasks are constituted matters as much as the material itself for producing understanding; tasks should be designed to reorganize informal and intuitive conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks to engage and help reorganize students’ informal concept images (e.g., for Euler’s method, equilibrium, stability) and ensure long-term coherence across task sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment fairness and content validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop routine and conceptual assessments so they are fair for all students by not including items unique to a particular curriculum emphases (e.g., dynamical-systems-specific topics) and by having content experts review items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask external mathematicians with differential equations expertise to review items; remove items at sites where topics were not covered; document validity and reliability (refer to prior work for details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Views About Mathematics Survey (VAMS) dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs instrument items grouped into philosophical dimensions (structure of mathematical knowledge, methods of mathematics, validity of mathematical knowledge) and pedagogical dimensions (learnability of mathematics, role of reflective thinking, personal relevance of mathematics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each VAMS item pairs two contrasting alternatives balanced on a five-point scale; administer pre- and post-instruction to detect changes in student beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine assessment (skills) coverage and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine assessment comprised analytic problems (e.g., separation of variables), one numerical Euler’s method problem, one phase plane graph sketching problem, and one modeling problem; maximum score on each problem = 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administering routine items as part of a regular final encourages student effort; however, relying on instructors to select which of the eight items to include can reduce experimental control—document which items used at each site when analyzing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual assessment (relational understanding) coverage and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual assessment consisted of eight items aimed at relational understandings: two on exact vs approximate solutions, two on modeling aspects, and four on behavior/structure of solutions and solution space; administered to volunteers for 60 minutes after finals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If particular conceptual items were not covered in a comparison class, remove those items for that site (as done at the Korean site); ensure comparability when interpreting cross-site results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind scoring with rubrics and inter-rater resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop rubrics for scoring routine and conceptual assessments; remove student names so scoring is blind; two project team members score each problem and a third resolves unreconciled differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protocol supports scoring reliability; report scoring procedures and inter-rater adjudication method when presenting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline comparability (prior mathematics background)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect baseline data on students’ previous mathematical understanding (e.g., CSAT, SAT math score, averaged calculus grades) and test for comparability (t-tests) between treatment and comparison groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude students missing baseline data from analyses; use baseline as covariate (ANCOVA) when analyzing posttest scores to adjust for pretest differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome criteria: routine skills vs conceptual understanding vs beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate effects on (a) students’ mathematical views (VAMS), (b) routine procedural skills (routine assessment), and (c) relational/conceptual understanding (conceptual assessment); IO-DE predicted to foster conceptual development while possibly matching routine skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report adjusted posttest means with pretest covariates; conduct item-by-item analyses; interpret where IO-DE may outperform (e.g., Euler’s method, conceptual items) and where no significant difference appears (e.g., many analytic problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological limitations and sample-size/power considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limitations such as sample size affecting power to detect differences, incomplete baseline data, and unequal administration conditions across sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend larger samples, inclusion of interviews for richer qualitative data, and more controlled administration for future studies to strengthen causal claims and cross-site comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of assessment items by instructors for fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: When routine assessment items are placed onto instructors’ final exams, allow instructors to select which of the eight items they feel are fair for their students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this increases perceived fairness and instructor goodwill, it reduces experimental control; document selections and consider their impact on comparability and analysis.
